title: Depth-First Search (DFS), Graph Connectivity, and Cycle Detection
description: Master Depth-First Search: recursive and iterative stack traversals, visited tracking, pre-order and post-order processing, connected components, and cycle detection.

sections.title: Depth-First Search mechanics: Recursive call stack traversal
sections.learning_objective: Traverse graph branches to maximum depth using recursive exploration.
sections.markdown:
## When to recognize this pattern
Exploring all paths, detecting cycles in graphs, connected component discovery, topological sort, or tree depth calculations.

## Core idea
`Depth-First Search` (`DFS`) explores a tree or graph by plunging down a single path as deeply as possible before `backtracking` to explore unvisited branches. The most natural `implementation` is `recursive`: the language runtime `call stack` automatically manages the exploration frontier. To prevent infinite loops in graphs with cycles, we maintain a `visited` collection. DFS explores every reachable `connected` vertex and edge in linear $O(V + E)$ time.

examples.explanation: Dives along path A -> B -> D before backtracking to explore C in O(V + E) time.
examples.expected_output:
Visited: A
Visited: B
Visited: D
Visited: C

key_points: DFS explores as deep as possible along each branch before backtracking.
In graphs, a visited set is mandatory to prevent infinite loops in cycles.

sections.title: Iterative DFS using an explicit stack
sections.learning_objective: Convert recursive DFS to an iterative algorithm to avoid call stack limits.
sections.markdown:
## Naive approach
Re-exploring already visited nodes creates infinite loops on cyclic graphs or exponential redundant computation.

## Better approach
In production environments with deep graphs (thousands of vertices), recursive DFS risks crashing with `RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded`. An `iterative` DFS simulates the call stack using an explicit `stack` data structure (a Python list). Push the start node onto the `stack`. While the stack is not empty, `pop` the top node, process it, and push all its unvisited neighbors. This executes on the heap, allowing traversal of graphs with millions of nodes without stack overflow.

examples.explanation: Iterative DFS using explicit list stack avoiding Python call stack depth limits.

key_points: Iterative DFS uses an explicit stack, bypassing call stack recursion limits.
Reversing neighbors before pushing preserves standard left-to-right order.
sections.checkpoint: Why does pushing neighbors in reverse order preserve left-to-right traversal order in an iterative stack?

sections.title: Pre-order and post-order processing in DFS
sections.learning_objective: Leverage pre-order and post-order timing in recursive algorithms.
sections.markdown:
## Python implementation
Recursive DFS uses the runtime call stack with a visited set, while iterative DFS manages an explicit list stack.

## Step-by-step example
In DFS, *when* an operation is executed relative to the recursive calls determines its category:
1. `pre-order`: Executed *before* visiting children (top-down propagation, such as passing path prefixes or parent values down the tree).
2. In-order (binary trees only): Executed *between* left and right children (produces sorted order in a Binary Search Tree).
3. `post-order`: Executed *after* visiting children (bottom-up aggregation, such as calculating subtree heights, max depth, or topological sorting where a node is recorded after all its dependencies finish).

examples.explanation: Demonstrates post-order bottom-up calculation of binary tree height.

key_points: Pre-order processes parents before children (top-down passing of context).
Post-order computes subproblem values from children before resolving the parent (bottom-up aggregation).

sections.title: Connected components and cycle detection in graphs
sections.learning_objective: Count connected components and identify cycles in directed graphs.
sections.markdown:
## Time complexity
O(V + E) on graphs or O(N) on trees, traversing every reachable vertex and edge exactly once.

## Space complexity
O(H) auxiliary space on trees where H is height; O(V) for the visited set and recursion stack on arbitrary graphs.

## Common mistakes
DFS solves core graph structural questions:
1. `connected` Components: Iterate through all vertices $0 \dots V-1$. If a vertex has not been visited, increment component count and launch DFS to mark its entire reachable component.
2. Cycle Detection (Directed Graphs): A simple `visited` set is insufficient for directed graphs because crossing paths is legal (e.g. Diamond graphs). We use 3-state coloring:
   - 0 (Unvisited)
   - 1 (Visiting: currently on the active recursion call stack)
   - 2 (Visited: completely processed)
If DFS encounters a neighbor currently in state 1 (Visiting), a cycle/back-edge is detected!

examples.explanation: Detects cycle in directed course prerequisites graph using 3-state DFS coloring.

key_points: Outer loop over all vertices ensures disconnected components are fully explored.
3-state coloring (unvisited, visiting, visited) reliably detects cycles in directed graphs.

sections.learning_objective: Solve DFS graph, tree, and grid problems in Coding Arena.
sections.markdown:
## Arena reference
Practice with `dsa-max-depth-tree` in Forge Arena. Restate the invariant and derive your solution independently before submitting to deterministic grading.

DFS questions test recursion control, state tracking, and base case formulation.

### Common Interview Questions
1. *What is the difference between DFS space complexity on a balanced tree vs skewed tree?*
   *(On a balanced tree, maximum depth is O(log N). On a skewed tree [degenerate list], maximum depth is O(N))*. 
2. *How does topological sorting relate to DFS post-order traversal?*
   *(In a Directed Acyclic Graph [DAG], reversing the post-order finishing times of DFS yields a valid topological sort order)*. 
3. *How do you solve Flood Fill on a 2D matrix using DFS?*
   *(Recurse in 4 cardinal directions, modifying cell color in-place to act as the visited marker)*. 

### Arena Practice Problems
- `dsa-max-depth-tree`: Post-order tree height traversal
- `dsa-number-of-islands-bfs`: DFS/BFS 2D grid component traversal
- `dsa-course-schedule`: Directed graph cycle detection and topological sorting

examples.code:
# 2D Grid Flood Fill using DFS
def flood_fill(image, sr, sc, new_color):
    orig = image[sr][sc]
    if orig == new_color: return image
    R, C = len(image), len(image[0])
    def dfs(r, c):
        if 0 <= r < R and 0 <= c < C and image[r][c] == orig:
            image[r][c] = new_color
            dfs(r + 1, c); dfs(r - 1, c); dfs(r, c + 1); dfs(r, c - 1)
    dfs(sr, sc)
    return image

img = [[1, 1, 1], [1, 1, 0], [1, 0, 1]]
print(flood_fill(img, 1, 1, 2))
examples.explanation: Executes 4-directional flood fill recursion in-place on 2D image matrix.

key_points: Practice both recursive and iterative DFS implementations.
In 2D grid DFS, guard against recursion on already-recolored cells to prevent infinite loops.

summary: DFS explores branches to maximum depth using recursive call stacks or iterative stack buffers.
Executes in linear O(V + E) time across graph vertices and edges.
Pre-order processes top-down before child recursion; post-order aggregates bottom-up after child recursion.
3-state coloring (unvisited, visiting, visited) detects cycles in directed graphs.
Iterative DFS eliminates recursion depth limits by managing an explicit heap stack.
interview_takeaways: Mention iterative DFS with an explicit stack if input tree height can exceed 1000 nodes in Python.
Explain pre-order vs post-order clearly when computing tree properties or topological orders.
Use 3-state coloring to prove cycle detection mastery on directed graph problems.
common_mistakes: Forgetting a visited set in cyclic graphs, causing infinite recursion loops and stack overflow
Using 2-state visited checking for cycle detection in directed graphs (falsely flagging cross-edges as cycles)
Overlooking disconnected graph components by only running DFS from vertex 0
Modifying global state across branches without restoring it
